report:
## Conclusion: The evidence points to "yes," not "no"

The premise that CT screening does **not** reduce lung-cancer mortality in heavy (ex-)smokers is contradicted by the best available randomized evidence.

**Key trials:**
- **NLST (US, ~53,000 high-risk smokers/ex-smokers, ≥30 pack-years)**: Annual low-dose CT reduced lung-cancer mortality by 20% and all-cause mortality by ~7% versus chest X-ray screening (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873).
- **NELSON (Dutch-Belgian, ~15,800 heavy smokers/ex-smokers)**: Volume CT screening reduced lung-cancer mortality by 24% in men and an even larger relative reduction in women at 10 years, confirming and strengthening NLST's findings (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793).

**Synthesis across trials:** The USPSTF's evidence review, pooling NELSON with other European trials, found reduced incidence rate ratios for lung-cancer death (~0.75, i.e., a 25% relative reduction) with roughly 130 people needing screening over 10 years to prevent one lung-cancer death (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/evidence-summary14/lung-cancer-screening). A 2022 Cochrane review of eight trials (91,122 participants) likewise concluded LDCT screening reduces lung-cancer mortality, though it noted heterogeneity and false-positive/overdiagnosis harms.

**Caveats/nuance:** Some earlier European trials (DANTE, DLCST, MILD, LUSI) were individually underpowered and showed non-significant or mixed results, which fueled early skepticism (as reflected in some meta-analyses and the "NNT" critique). However, once adequately powered (NLST, NELSON) or pooled, results consistently show a real, moderate mortality benefit specifically in heavy current/former smokers meeting eligibility criteria (typically ≥20-30 pack-years).

**Bottom line:** Current high-quality randomized trial evidence supports that regular LDCT screening does reduce lung-cancer mortality among heavy (ex-)smokers, which is why USPSTF recommends it for this group—contradicting a "no" answer, though benefits come with real harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, radiation) that must be weighed.
